miniProject.title: Telemetry, a load sweep through the knee, overload control and one incident
miniProject.brief: Make the service slice measurable and keep it upright past its capacity: instrument the request path, predict the knee from measured service time, sweep through it with an open-loop generator, add overload controls, then inject one incident, recover from the runbook and write the postmortem. The SLO, capacity and 10x plan go into the dossier.
steps: Instrument every request with request ID, trace context, queue wait, handler time, storage time (write plus fsync), status and bounded labels (operation, status class, protocol version). Write telemetry to JSON Lines files: one raw record per request kept for the whole run, plus counters and fixed-bucket latency histograms (for example 1, 3, 10, 30 ms and so on to 3 s). Enforce a cardinality budget in a test: the product of label value counts must stay under your declared limit, so adding a client ID label fails it; client IDs live on sampled trace records only.

Predict before measuring. From the mean service time \(S\) measured at one worker, capacity is at most \(\text{workers}/S\), and lower if fsync calls serialize on the one log file; batching acknowledgements behind one fsync (group commit) raises it. Write the predicted knee and the queue length Little's Law gives at 50%, 80% and 95% of that capacity.

Write an open-loop generator: a seeded Poisson schedule computed in advance, latency measured from the intended send time, every raw record kept. Sweep at least five offered rates from well below to past the predicted knee, drop a warm-up and repeat each rate three times. Report \(p_{50}\), \(p_{95}\) and \(p_{99}\) from raw samples with \(n\), throughput, goodput, queue depth, utilization and errors, check \(L = \lambda W\) against sampled queue depth, and measure recovery time after the overload stops. Run the closed-loop twin at one rate and explain why it hides the tail.

Write the SLO: an availability SLI (good over valid requests) and a latency SLI (the fraction under a threshold), a 30-day target with its budget (99.9% allows 43.2 minutes), the alert you would page on and the failure domains the single node shares (disk, host, power). Derive capacity at a 0.7 utilization target now and at 10x load, and what you would shed, degrade or remove instead of only adding machines.

Add overload controls and show each one under the same injected overload, with goodput and \(p_{99}\) with and without it: bounded admission with an overloaded error, client-side adaptive throttling from the client's own request and accept counts (\(K = 2\) as in the SRE book), a per-client retry budget (the unit uses 5% of requests) with jittered backoff, a breaker on the store call whose fallback serves cached reads marked stale, and deadline propagation with cancellation.

Add a version flag and a canary split: send a declared fraction of requests to the new version, compare its error rate and p99 with the stable version over the same window, and roll back automatically when either crosses its threshold. Test the rollback with a deliberately slow version.

Inject one incident whose cause a script picks from a seeded list, so you do not know it in advance: a corrupted log record, slow fsync from a container started with --device-write-bps, or a bad canary. Work it from the telemetry and the runbook: a timeline with detection, diagnosis, mitigation and recovery times, a restore from the last verified backup with measured RTO and counted RPO loss (writes acknowledged after the backup), a blameless postmortem with owned actions and one merged regression guard.
deliverables: The instrumented service with telemetry files, the cardinality test and a script that renders percentiles and queue depth from the raw records.
The load sweep: prediction, raw records, the table at every rate, the Little's Law check and the closed-loop comparison.
The overload-control and canary experiments, each with numbers with and without the control.
The SLO and capacity page and the incident package: timeline, runbook, restore evidence with RTO and RPO, postmortem and regression guard.

rubric.pass: Every request has a raw record with request ID, queue wait, handler and storage time and status, and the cardinality test fails on an unbounded label.
rubric.strong: Percentiles come only from raw samples or merged histogram counts, never from averaged percentiles, and the report says which.

rubric.pass: The knee was predicted before the sweep, and the sweep reports percentiles with \(n\), goodput, queue depth and utilization at every rate with the Little's Law check.
rubric.strong: The measured knee is explained against the prediction, including any fsync serialization the prediction missed.

rubric.pass: Each control is shown under the same injected overload, with goodput and p99 with and without it.
rubric.strong: The retry budget and throttle are shown stopping a retry storm that the plain retrying client starts.

rubric.pass: The incident has a timeline, a runbook-driven recovery, measured RTO, counted RPO loss and a merged regression guard.
rubric.strong: The postmortem is blameless with owned, dated actions, and the runbook was followed cold by someone else or by you a day later.

rubric.pass: The SLO, error budget, alert and 10x plan are written with the arithmetic shown.
rubric.strong: The plan names the failure domains the single node shares and what the SLO cannot promise because of them.

miniProject.feedsInto: Capstone dossier: the SLO and capacity estimate against load and the telemetry-based incident. Service slice: bounded admission, deadlines and overload controls under test.
